content: The parts-per notation is a method commonly used in scientific and engineering disciplines to represent relative proportions in measured quantities. It is particularly useful for expressing very small proportions, such as parts-per-million (ppm), parts-per-billion (ppb), and parts-per-trillion (ppt). These notations are dimensionless quantities, meaning they are pure numbers without associated units of measurement. In written language, parts-per is often interpreted as a comparative ratio, while in mathematical expressions, it functions as a coefficient with values less than 1. In chemistry, the parts-per notation is frequently employed to measure dilutions or concentrations, such as the relative abundance of dissolved minerals or pollutants in water. For example, 1 ppm indicates that a specific property exists at a ratio of one part per million parts of the sample. This could represent a waterborne pollutant present at a concentration of one-millionth of a gram per gram of the solution. Similarly, this notation is used in physics and engineering to describe proportional phenomena, as well as to quantify changes, stability, or uncertainty in measurements. Although the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) recognizes the use of parts-per notation, it is not formally part of the International System of Units (SI). Furthermore, due to differences in the interpretation of large numbers (e.g., billion can mean 10⁹ or 10¹² depending on the country), the BIPM advises against using ppb and ppt to avoid confusion. Despite this, ppm remains widely used in technical fields because of its convenience in representing dimensionless quantities. The parts-per expressions can be broken down as follows: 1. One part per hundred (percent, %): This represents one part per 100 parts, equivalent to a value of 1 × 10⁻². For example, it is comparable to one drop of water diluted into 5 milliliters or one second of time in 1 minute and 40 seconds. 2. One part per thousand (‰): This denotes one part per 1,000 parts, equivalent to 1 × 10⁻³. It is similar to one drop of water diluted into 50 milliliters or one second of time in 16 minutes and 40 seconds. The abbreviation ppt should be avoided here, as it can also mean parts per trillion. 3. One part per ten thousand (‱): Represented by the permyriad symbol, this is primarily used in finance to denote fractional changes in percentages, such as basis points. It corresponds to one part per 10,000 parts, or 1 × 10⁻⁴. This is equivalent to one drop of water diluted into half a liter or one second of time in approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes. 4. One part per million (ppm): This indicates one part per 1,000,000 parts, or 1 × 10⁻⁶. It is equivalent to one drop of water diluted into 50 liters (roughly the fuel tank capacity of a compact car) or one second of time in approximately 11.5 days. 5. One part per billion (ppb): This represents one part per 1,000,000,000 parts, or 1 × 10⁻⁹. It is equivalent to one drop of water diluted into a large swimming pool or one second of time in approximately 31.7 years. 6. One part per trillion (ppt): This denotes one part per 1,000,000,000,000 parts, or 1 × 10⁻¹². It is comparable to one drop of water diluted into 20 Olympic-sized swimming pools or one second of time in approximately 31,700 years. 7. One part per quadrillion (ppq): This represents one part per 1,000,000,000,000,000 parts, or 1 × 10⁻¹⁵. It is equivalent to one drop of water diluted into a vast volume or one second of time in approximately 31.7 million years. The BIPM advises caution when using ppb, ppt, and ppq due to potential misunderstandings arising from language differences and varying numerical conventions. For example, the term billion can mean different values depending on whether the long or short scale is used. While the short scale is now dominant in English-speaking countries, the long scale remains prevalent in many non-English-speaking regions. To address the challenges of expressing dimensionless quantities, the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics (IUPAP) proposed the adoption of the term uno (symbol: U) in 1999 to represent the number 1 in dimensionless quantities. This unit could theoretically be combined with SI prefixes to express values much smaller or larger than one. However, the uno has not been adopted by any standards organization and is unlikely to become an officially sanctioned method for expressing low-value dimensionless quantities. It is important to note that parts-per notation should only be used for true dimensionless quantities, where the units of measurement cancel out, leaving a pure number. Mixed-unit quantities, such as 15 pCi/L for radon concentration, are not dimensionless and should not be expressed using parts-per notation. In technical writing, especially in contexts like drinking water reports, clarity and ease of understanding for the intended audience are paramount. For example, contamination levels in drinking water are often expressed on a per-liter basis, as this aligns with the public's intuitive understanding of volumetric quantities. Finally, parts-per notations can be converted into other units of the same measure without altering the relative proportion they represent. For instance, a metering pump injecting a trace chemical at a proportional flow rate of 125 ppm can also be expressed as 125 µL/L, 125 µgal/gal, or 125 µ(m³)/m³, depending on the chosen volumetric unit.
